title: All by Yourself
mood: A cut kept secret, a match fought with one arm, a new rule between partners, and two felt dolls finished at last.

hero.alt: Under a smoky gray sky, pink-haired Guinevere and black-haired Vexana in school uniform stand back to back, Guinevere's gloved fist raised, Vexana's violet eyes fixed ahead.

segs.t: Vexana stood with her back to Guinevere’s in a street of shut shops by the seawall. It was the fifth raid in nine days. She had counted from the siren on the dormitory roof.
Since the newcomers came, the raids had grown fiercer. Each one came down a little nearer the Academy’s own waterfront. Every time, the two of them stood at the front. Guinevere liked the front.
To Vexana’s eye, more Enders turned toward Guinevere than toward anyone.
They go for the strongest,
she thought.
She did not say it. Guinevere would only take it as praise. Vexana kept a step nearer her back instead, as she had since the fish market.
An Ender dropped off a roof on Guinevere’s left, her open side. Its chest plates split for the strike. Guinevere’s fist was already deep in another one’s core. She did not see it.
There was no time to aim. Vexana stepped in.

The claw struck her staff and skidded down it. It tore her left glove at the wrist and opened the arm above it. She pressed the orb to the bare core and fired. The Ender went over backward onto the stones.
“Did you get it?” Guinevere called, without turning round.
“Yes.”
Her arm burned. Under the burn was something she had not expected.
That was easier than watching it hit her,
she thought.

That night she shut her door and dressed the cut at her desk. It was long, and not deep. She had dressed her own cuts since she was small. She wound the bandage tight from the wrist up, pushed the torn glove to the bottom of a drawer and pulled on her spare pair. The cuff came over the bandage, and the sleeve came over the cuff.
It came at her open side,
she thought.
If she knows, she’ll start looking back.
Guinevere fought the way she did because she never looked back.
Her father’s toolbox stood by the desk. It still smelled of gun oil.
He came back for me, and paid for it,
she thought.
This one I pay myself.
So for four days Vexana said nothing. She did her fifty forms every morning. On the runs she kept her left arm in close against her side.
Four days after the seawall, sparring in the training hall, Guinevere caught Vexana’s wrist.
It was a good catch. It usually went the other way: Vexana’s hand on her wrist, at the edge of a roof.
Vexana flinched.
Vexana never flinched. Guinevere looked down. The white glove had slid back, and under its cuff a bandage was wound tight round the arm. Blood had come through it.
Guinevere kept hold. She turned the cuff back further. The bandage ran on up under the sleeve.
The street by the seawall.
Did you get it?
Yes.
Four days of that arm held in close on the runs.
I didn’t even turn round,
she thought.
“First the library. Now this.” Her voice went up. “You did it again. All by yourself.”
“It was mine to carry,” said Vexana.
Mine,
thought Guinevere.
As if there were only one of us.
“I was right there,” she said. “Four days. And you didn’t need me for any of it.”
Vexana did not answer.
Guinevere let go of the wrist. Her hand was shaking, so she made it into a fist.
“Let’s settle this with a match, Vexana.”
Vexana looked at her.
“Tonight. Here.” Guinevere pointed at the floor. “Medic first.”
That night the training hall was empty. Guinevere lit only the lamp at its center.
Vexana came on the minute, with her practice staff. A clean white dressing showed at the cuff of her glove.
Guinevere tucked her own left hand into the back of her belt. “One arm each. Fair.”
“You fight with both.”
“Tonight I fight with one.” Her chin went up. “If I win, you tell me first. Every cut. Every paper.”
“If I win?”
“You won’t.”
Her drones rose at her shoulders. She lifted her one fist.
“Prepare yourself.”
She came in fast, a drone wide on each side. The staff met her fist, then swept at her knees. She jumped it. A drone dived at Vexana’s head, and the staff turned it away without a look.
Face to face, neither could fool the other. Guinevere had felt that staff at her back for most of a year.
Guinevere kept to the right. She never once went for the left arm.
Sweat ran into her eyes. Her drones had sunk to her elbows. She was grinning, and could not remember when she had started.
She hooked a heel behind Vexana’s ankle. In the same moment the staff hooked hers. They went down together, flat on their backs on the hall floor, side by side.
Neither got up. They lay there and breathed.
One drone sagged out of the air and sat down on Guinevere’s stomach.
“Traitor,” she told it.
Beside her, Vexana laughed.
It was short, and rusty. Guinevere turned her head on the floor and stared. She had seen Vexana smile. She had never heard her laugh.
Vexana looked as startled by it as she was.
“A draw,” said Guinevere, to the roof beams. “So we both make the rule. Partners tell each other first. Both of us.”
For a moment she thought of the bench outside her father’s office, and a paper held up to the gap in his door. That paper she kept to herself.
“Rules are for keeping safe what matters,” said Vexana.
“I said that.”
“I know,” said Vexana. “I kept it.”
The drone hummed on Guinevere’s stomach.
“First,” said Vexana.
Guinevere spread her one free arm out across the cold floor. “As long as we’re together, nothing’s too heavy.”
A new plan came under Vexana’s door before the bells, a whole month of it. Three colors of ink, as always. Across the top, in gold:
Partners tell each other first.
At the run Guinevere fell in beside her, still yawning. They were past the fountain before Vexana spoke.
“My arm aches today.”
Guinevere stopped dead on the path. Then she threw both arms in the air. “Thank you for telling me first!” she shouted, to the whole path.
“You’re shouting.”
“I’m thrilled.”

On the board outside the Combat office, the new watch sheet had gone up. From tomorrow, for a week, the Investigation Room watch was theirs. That was the wing where the Science Division took Ender wreckage apart, to learn how it worked.
“A week guarding broken Enders,” said Guinevere. “How heroic.”
“Someone has to.”
That evening they took two red cups of tea up to the dormitory roof. The sun was going down behind the dome’s curve, and the whole city had turned orange.
Guinevere leaned on the green rail. Her left bow had slipped again. It always slipped by evening.
Every morning since the ceremony, Vexana had set it straight before the run. Now she reached over and set it straight again. Guinevere did not stop talking.
“...and out there.” She pointed over the roofs, toward the dome’s edge where the houses ended. “The fireworks. Same place. Next year.”
“Same place,” said Vexana.
Guinevere swung round. “You didn’t say ‘if.’”
“No.”
“We think alike!”
Vexana turned the red cup in her hands. “True partners don’t just think alike, they complete each other.”
Guinevere looked at her and said nothing at all. Then she knocked her cup against Vexana’s, and tea slopped over the rim onto the white glove.
That night Vexana sewed the last stitch.

She had worked on the dolls since the summer, a few stitches at a time, the bad ones picked out. She had no red felt, so the pink-haired one wore two bows of red thread. Each had a tiny star at its collar, in yellow thread.
She stood them beside the photo frame on her desk, a pink-haired Guinevere and a black-haired Vexana.
She wrote a card in small square letters, in Guinevere’s own words from the roof, and propped it under them.
For Guinevere. Same place, next year.
She would give them at the fireworks.
The month’s plan lay beside them, the gold line at the top. Vexana read it again.
A present doesn’t count,
she decided.
Across the grounds the training hall was still lit. She dialed.
“Go to bed.”
“I’m asleep.”
Guinevere had not said that since the first night.
“You’re in the training hall.”
A pause. “...I’m going.”
Down the line, the hall door banged shut. Vexana put the phone down beside the dolls.
